It is hard to **maintain** standards.

vocab.definition: Kept in good condition or at the same level.
examples: Trials found productivity was **maintained**.
The garden is well **maintained**.

vocab.definition: The desire to harm or cause suffering to others.
examples: The conflict stemmed from misunderstanding rather than **malice**.
She bore him no **malice**.

vocab.definition: Intending or intended to do harm.
examples: His jokes are never **malicious**.
It was a **malicious** rumour.

vocab.definition: Harmful or evil in nature or influence.
examples: The technology is not inherently **malign**.
It had a **malign** influence.

vocab.definition: Able to be dealt with or controlled without difficulty.
examples: Break large tasks into smaller, **manageable** steps.
The workload is **manageable**.

vocab.definition: The process of controlling or dealing with things or people.
examples: They require careful **management**.
Good time **management** is vital.

vocab.definition: Controlling or influencing someone unfairly or deviously.
examples: Data can be used for **manipulation** on a mass scale.
Emotional **manipulation** is damaging.

vocab.definition: Artificially created or produced, not natural or genuine.
examples: Consumption is driven by **manufactured** wants.
The crisis was **manufactured**.

vocab.definition: Treated as insignificant or pushed to the edges of society.
examples: Anyone facing barriers to contact is **marginalised**.
Minority groups are often **marginalised**.

vocab.definition: Comprehensive skill or command of a subject.
examples: His discipline turned potential into real **mastery**.
She achieved **mastery** of the language.

vocab.definition: To be equal to or as good as something.
examples: It set a standard that has been hard to **match**.
Nothing can **match** a home-cooked meal.

vocab.definition: Relating to physical possessions rather than the spiritual.
examples: People seem content despite fewer **material** comforts.
He cares little for **material** wealth.

vocab.definition: Overly concerned with money and possessions.
examples: Something more **materialistic** is being questioned.
He grew increasingly **materialistic**.

vocab.definition: In a sensible, adult and well-considered way.
examples: Healthy relationships handle disagreement **maturely**.
She reacted **maturely**.

vocab.definition: Making something as great or large as possible.
examples: He reinvested profits rather than **maximising** his own wealth.
The firm focuses on **maximising** output.

vocab.definition: Significance, purpose or the sense of something.
examples: They give life a certain **meaning** and rhythm.
She searched for **meaning** in her work.

vocab.definition: Having serious, important or worthwhile significance.
examples: I wanted to give her something genuinely **meaningful**.
It was a **meaningful** gesture.

vocab.definition: In a way that has real significance or purpose.
examples: We interact more frequently yet less **meaningfully**.
They engaged **meaningfully** with the issue.

vocab.definition: A neutral person who helps others resolve a dispute.
examples: I acted as a neutral **mediator**.
A **mediator** helped settle the dispute.

vocab.definition: Involving deep, calm and reflective thought.
examples: Walking there is genuinely **meditative**.
She has a **meditative** quality.

vocab.definition: A means or channel by which something is communicated.
examples: The core need is universal, but the **medium** has shifted.
Television is a powerful **medium**.

vocab.definition: A feeling of pensive, thoughtful sadness.
examples: I still find it a little **melancholy**.
A sense of **melancholy** hung over the day.

vocab.definition: Worth remembering; not easily forgotten.
examples: It turned into a strangely **memorable** adventure.
It was a **memorable** trip.

vocab.definition: The faculty of recalling; a thing remembered.
examples: A solid base of knowledge in your own **memory** is essential.
It is a treasured **memory**.

vocab.definition: Experienced people who advise and guide others.
examples: A young leader would be paired with experienced **mentors**.
Good **mentors** shape careers.

vocab.definition: The quality of being good or deserving; worth.
examples: Fame has become disconnected from genuine **merit**.
The idea has real **merit**.

vocab.definition: Completely captivated and holding one's attention.
examples: We were all completely **mesmerised**.
The children sat **mesmerised**.

vocab.definition: Capturing one's attention completely; hypnotic.
examples: Watching him perform is genuinely **mesmerising**.
The dance was **mesmerising**.

vocab.definition: Done in an orderly, systematic and careful way.
examples: She is **methodical**, planning so nothing slips through.
He took a **methodical** approach.

vocab.definition: Controlling every small detail of a task or person's work.
examples: Companies should trust employees rather than **micromanaging** them.
He kept **micromanaging** the team.

vocab.definition: A significant stage or event in progress or development.
examples: Owning a car would feel like a real **milestone**.
Graduation is an important **milestone**.

vocab.definition: To imitate or copy, often closely.
examples: AI can **mimic** these qualities but not replicate them.
He can **mimic** any accent.

vocab.definition: Conscious or aware of something; attentive.
examples: I'm trying to be more **mindful** of my consumption.
Be **mindful** of the risks.

vocab.definition: In a conscious, attentive and deliberate way.
examples: Used **mindfully**, the benefits can outweigh the drawbacks.
She spends her time **mindfully**.

vocab.definition: Done without thought or attention; requiring no intelligence.
examples: Endless scrolling can be **mindless**.
It was **mindless** entertainment.

vocab.definition: Remarkable and almost impossible to believe; wonderful.
examples: It felt almost **miraculous** that a device could bridge the gap.
Her recovery was **miraculous**.

vocab.definition: An inaccurate or misleading description of something.
examples: I think it is a **mischaracterisation** to call people selfish.
That is a **mischaracterisation** of the facts.

vocab.definition: A failure to communicate ideas or intentions clearly.
examples: Simple **miscommunication** is a common trigger of conflict.
The error was due to **miscommunication**.

vocab.definition: Very unhappy or uncomfortable.
examples: A secure but **miserable** job harms mental health.
He looked utterly **miserable**.

vocab.definition: A state of great unhappiness or suffering.
examples: Financial security can remove a major source of **misery**.
Poverty causes great **misery**.

vocab.definition: Based on faulty judgement or mistaken reasoning.
examples: Equating success with money seems **misguided**.
It was a well-meant but **misguided** effort.

vocab.definition: To understand something wrongly.
examples: The absence of tone makes messages easy to **misinterpret**.
Don't **misinterpret** my silence.

vocab.definition: Caused someone to have a wrong idea or belief.
examples: People risk being dangerously gullible or **misled**.
The advert **misled** customers.

vocab.definition: A failure to correspond or be suitable.
examples: There is often a **mismatch** between skills and needs.
The result was a **mismatch** of expectations.

vocab.definition: A failure to understand something correctly.
examples: Most conflict stems from **misunderstanding**.
It was a simple **misunderstanding**.

vocab.definition: To make something less severe, serious or harmful.
examples: Prioritising sustainability can **mitigate** the harm.
Steps to **mitigate** the risk were taken.

vocab.definition: The ability to move or to change social status.
examples: Free education promotes social **mobility**.
The injury reduced her **mobility**.

vocab.definition: A system or example used as a basis for imitation.
examples: The old **model** of lifelong loyalty is outdated.
It became a **model** for others.

vocab.definition: Demonstrating behaviour for others to imitate.
examples: The most effective way is by **modelling** those values.
Parents are **modelling** good habits.

vocab.definition: The avoidance of excess or extremes.
examples: Video games are beneficial in **moderation**.
Everything is fine in **moderation**.

vocab.definition: Relating to the present or recent times; contemporary.
examples: It manages to be both **modern** and timeless.
**Modern** life is fast-paced.

vocab.definition: Brought up to date with current methods or ideas.
examples: Curricula should be **modernised** to include life skills.
The factory has been **modernised**.

vocab.definition: Made of separate parts or units that can be combined.
examples: There may be a shift towards shorter, **modular** courses.
The system has a **modular** design.

vocab.definition: The force or driving power gained by a movement or process.
examples: A strong leader gives a movement **momentum**.
The campaign gained **momentum**.

vocab.definition: Principles concerning right and wrong behaviour.
examples: Blind obedience can conflict with genuine **morality**.
It is a question of **morality**.

vocab.definition: To give someone a reason or enthusiasm to act.
examples: Ambitious peers can **motivate** you to raise your standards.
Good teachers **motivate** students.

vocab.definition: Enthusiastic and driven to achieve something.
examples: Under her, the team was noticeably more **motivated**.
She is highly **motivated**.

vocab.definition: The reason or drive for behaving in a particular way.
examples: Self-**motivation** is the biggest challenge in independent learning.
She lacks **motivation**.

vocab.definition: Looking or smelling extremely appetising.
examples: The aromas alone were **mouthwatering**.
The menu was **mouthwatering**.

vocab.definition: Affected with strong emotion.
examples: By the end, I was genuinely **moved**.
She was deeply **moved** by the gesture.

vocab.definition: Arousing strong emotion, especially sadness or sympathy.
examples: Visiting it is a genuinely **moving** experience.
It was a **moving** tribute.

vocab.definition: Having many aspects or sides.
examples: Crime is a complex, **multifaceted** issue.
She has a **multifaceted** career.

vocab.definition: In a way that is shared or done by two or more parties.
examples: Prosperity and welfare are **mutually** reinforcing.
The arrangement is **mutually** beneficial.

vocab.definition: Limited in extent, range or scope; not wide.
examples: Growing up in a small town gave me a rather **narrow** view of the world.
The course covers a **narrow** but very specialised area of law.

vocab.definition: Existing in or produced by nature; unforced and instinctive.
examples: She has a **natural** talent for putting nervous people at ease.
It felt like the most **natural** thing in the world to help him.

vocab.definition: The basic character or qualities of something; the physical world as a whole.
examples: The very **nature** of the job means you are always on call.
Spending time in **nature** is the fastest way for me to unwind.

vocab.definition: To find one's way through, or to deal successfully with, something complicated.
examples: Learning to **navigate** a new culture can be daunting at first.
Good managers help their teams **navigate** periods of uncertainty.

vocab.definition: Something that is essential rather than optional.
examples: In my city, owning a car is a **necessity** rather than a luxury.
Financial pressure turned frugality into an absolute **necessity**.

vocab.definition: The things a person requires in order to live or function well.
examples: A good education system should cater to the **needs** of every learner.
She always puts her family's **needs** before her own.

vocab.definition: A tendency to be pessimistic or to focus on the bad side of things.
examples: Constant **negativity** in the workplace can drain everyone's morale.
I try to filter out the **negativity** on social media.

vocab.definition: Not given the care or attention that is needed.
examples: The old building had been badly **neglected** for decades.
Many people feel their mental health is a **neglected** issue.

vocab.definition: Fails to give proper care or attention to something.
examples: A society that **neglects** its elderly loses something vital.
He often **neglects** his own health while caring for others.

vocab.definition: Anxious or worried, often before something important.
examples: I always get **nervous** before speaking in front of a crowd.
She was visibly **nervous** ahead of the interview.

vocab.definition: Remaining after all deductions; the overall result once everything is accounted for.
examples: The **net** effect of the policy was a rise in living costs.
Despite the setbacks, the **net** outcome was positive.

vocab.definition: Not supporting either side; impartial and unbiased.
examples: A referee has to stay completely **neutral** throughout the match.
I tried to keep my tone **neutral** so as not to sway anyone.

vocab.definition: Not open to discussion or change; fixed as a firm condition.
examples: For me, honesty in a friendship is **non-negotiable**.
Safety standards on site are strictly **non-negotiable**.

vocab.definition: A standard or pattern of behaviour that is typical or expected.
examples: Remote work has become the **norm** in many industries.
Social **norms** vary enormously from one culture to another.

vocab.definition: To make something become accepted as usual or standard.
examples: We need to **normalise** talking openly about failure.
The media has helped **normalise** flexible working.

vocab.definition: A sentimental longing for the past.
examples: Old songs fill me with a warm sense of **nostalgia**.
There is a wave of **nostalgia** for the technology of the nineties.

vocab.definition: Feeling or evoking a sentimental longing for the past.
examples: Looking through old photos always makes me **nostalgic**.
The film has a **nostalgic** charm that appeals to older viewers.

vocab.definition: To provide with what is needed to grow, thrive or stay healthy.
examples: Reading widely helps **nourish** a child's imagination.
A balanced diet **nourishes** both body and mind.

vocab.definition: Characterised by subtle distinctions or shades of meaning.
examples: It is a **nuanced** issue that resists simple answers.
Her essay offered a far more **nuanced** view than the headlines.

vocab.definition: Relating to the nucleus of an atom, or to the energy released from it.
examples: Some countries rely heavily on **nuclear** power for electricity.
The debate over **nuclear** energy is far from settled.

vocab.definition: To care for and encourage the growth or development of someone or something.
examples: Great teachers **nurture** curiosity rather than just deliver facts.
It takes patience to **nurture** a new business through its early years.

vocab.definition: Cared for and encouraged to grow or develop.
examples: A talent that is carefully **nurtured** can go a very long way.
She was **nurtured** in a home that valued reading above all.

vocab.definition: Providing care and encouragement for growth or development.
examples: Children flourish in a warm, **nurturing** environment.
He has a **nurturing** side that makes him a wonderful mentor.

vocab.definition: Compliance with an order, rule or authority.
examples: Strict **obedience** was expected in the schools of that era.
Blind **obedience** can be just as dangerous as outright rebellion.

vocab.definition: The condition of being severely overweight.
examples: Childhood **obesity** has become a serious public health concern.
Poor diet and inactivity are the main drivers of **obesity**.

vocab.definition: In a way based on facts rather than personal feelings or bias.
examples: It is hard to judge your own work **objectively**.
**Objectively** speaking, the data does not support that claim.

vocab.definition: A duty or commitment that one is bound to fulfil.
examples: I feel a strong **obligation** to support my parents as they age.
Companies have an **obligation** to protect their customers' data.

vocab.definition: Based on watching or noticing things rather than on experiment.
examples: Good comedians have sharp **observational** humour.
The study relied on **observational** data gathered over years.

vocab.definition: A person who watches or notices things, often keenly.
examples: As a quiet **observer**, I tend to notice details others miss.
To an outside **observer**, the system looks needlessly complex.

vocab.definition: A fixed preoccupation with something that dominates one's thoughts.
examples: Society's **obsession** with productivity can be exhausting.
His **obsession** with detail borders on the extreme.

vocab.definition: Preoccupied with something to an unreasonable or unhealthy degree.
examples: He is almost **obsessive** about keeping his desk tidy.
Social media can encourage an **obsessive** comparison with others.

vocab.definition: No longer produced or used; out of date.
examples: Some skills risk becoming **obsolete** as automation spreads.
Cassette players are now almost entirely **obsolete**.

vocab.definition: Something that blocks progress or makes it difficult.
examples: A lack of funding was the biggest **obstacle** we faced.
Fear of failure is often the only **obstacle** standing in our way.

vocab.definition: Things that block progress or make something difficult.
examples: She overcame enormous **obstacles** to get where she is.
Every worthwhile goal comes with its share of **obstacles**.

vocab.definition: A particular event, or a suitable time for something.
examples: A wedding is an **occasion** that brings the whole family together.
I save that suit for special **occasions** only.

vocab.definition: From time to time; not very often.
examples: I **occasionally** treat myself to a meal out.
We only see each other **occasionally** these days.

vocab.definition: Continuing; still in progress.
examples: Learning a language is an **ongoing** process, not a one-off task.
There is **ongoing** debate about the best way forward.

vocab.definition: Willing to consider new ideas and opinions.
examples: Travelling has made me far more **open-minded**.
An **open-minded** approach is essential in any negotiation.

vocab.definition: A favourable set of circumstances that makes something possible.
examples: Studying abroad was an **opportunity** I simply could not turn down.
A crisis can also be an **opportunity** to rethink things.

vocab.definition: Prolonged cruel or unjust treatment or control.
examples: The novel deals with themes of **oppression** and resistance.
Freedom of speech is a bulwark against **oppression**.

vocab.definition: Unjustly harsh or controlling; hard to bear.
examples: They lived under an **oppressive** regime for years.
The heat that afternoon was almost **oppressive**.

vocab.definition: Hopeful and confident about the future.
examples: Despite the setbacks, I remain **optimistic** about the outcome.
She has an infectiously **optimistic** outlook on life.

vocab.definition: A painful or very difficult experience.
examples: The whole trip turned into something of an **ordeal**.
She came through the **ordeal** stronger than before.

vocab.definition: Arranged in a systematic, orderly way; good at planning.
examples: Being naturally **organised** helps me juggle several projects.
The event was impressively well **organised**.

vocab.definition: Created directly and personally; new and inventive rather than copied.
examples: What I admire is her ability to come up with **original** ideas.
The **original** plan had to be scrapped entirely.

vocab.definition: Elaborately decorated.
examples: The palace was famous for its **ornate** ceilings.
I prefer clean lines to anything too **ornate**.

vocab.definition: No longer visible; hidden from view.
examples: Once the train was **out of sight**, the platform felt empty.
I keep my phone **out of sight** when I need to focus.

vocab.definition: Old-fashioned; no longer useful or relevant.
examples: Some teaching methods feel hopelessly **outdated** today.
The software was so **outdated** it could barely run.

vocab.definition: Unpleasantly domineering or controlling.
examples: An **overbearing** boss can crush a team's initiative.
He means well, but he can be a little **overbearing**.

vocab.definition: The state of having too many people in a space.
examples: **Overcrowding** on public transport is a daily frustration.
The city is struggling with housing **overcrowding**.

vocab.definition: A thorough examination and overhaul or reform of something.
examples: The system is badly in need of a complete **overhaul**.
The curriculum underwent a major **overhaul** last year.

vocab.definition: Having too much of something enjoyable, especially food or drink.
examples: It is easy to end up **overindulging** during the holidays.
I regretted **overindulging** at the buffet.

vocab.definition: Extremely happy.
examples: I was **overjoyed** when I heard I had passed.
They were **overjoyed** at the birth of their first child.

vocab.definition: Failed to notice or consider; ignored.
examples: Small acts of kindness are too often **overlooked**.
A crucial detail had been completely **overlooked**.

vocab.definition: To try to do or claim more than is wise or possible; excess of authority.
examples: Government **overreach** is a common concern in that debate.
Ambition is good, but it is easy to **overreach**.

vocab.definition: Takes precedence over; cancels out something else.
examples: In an emergency, safety **overrides** every other consideration.
Her sense of duty usually **overrides** her personal wishes.

vocab.definition: To be more prominent or important than, so as to make something seem less significant.
examples: One scandal can **overshadow** years of good work.
The sequel was **overshadowed** by the original film.

vocab.definition: The act of describing something as simpler than it really is.
examples: To blame it all on technology is an **oversimplification**.
That summary is an **oversimplification** of a complex issue.

vocab.definition: Made to seem simpler than it actually is.
examples: The report gave an **oversimplified** picture of the economy.
That argument feels rather **oversimplified** to me.

vocab.definition: Overcome by an excess of something, such as work or emotion.
examples: I sometimes feel **overwhelmed** by the sheer amount of information.
She was **overwhelmed** by the kindness of strangers.

vocab.definition: Very great in amount or effect; hard to resist or deal with.
examples: The response to the campaign was **overwhelming**.
There is **overwhelming** evidence to support the theory.

vocab.definition: Excessive work; to work too hard or make someone do so.
examples: Chronic **overwork** is a leading cause of burnout.
Managers should be careful not to **overwork** their staff.

vocab.definition: The state of owning something; taking responsibility for something.
examples: Home **ownership** is out of reach for many young people.
I like to take full **ownership** of my mistakes.

vocab.definition: Very crowded or full.
examples: The stadium was **packed** long before kick-off.
My schedule is completely **packed** this week.

vocab.definition: Great care or effort taken over something.
examples: She took great **pains** to make every guest feel welcome.
He went to considerable **pains** to get the details right.

vocab.definition: Sudden uncontrollable fear; to feel such fear.
examples: There was a moment of **panic** when the lights went out.
I tend to **panic** under tight deadlines.

vocab.definition: Offering a wide, unbroken view of a large area.
examples: The rooftop café has a **panoramic** view of the city.
From the summit you get a **panoramic** sweep of the valley.

vocab.definition: Unable to move or act, often through fear or indecision.
examples: I was **paralysed** with nerves before my first speech.
The city was **paralysed** by the sudden strike.

vocab.definition: Causing one to be unable to move or act.
examples: A **paralysing** fear of failure held her back for years.
The choice was so vast it became **paralysing**.

vocab.definition: More important than anything else; supreme.
examples: For any airline, passenger safety is **paramount**.
Trust is of **paramount** importance in a partnership.

vocab.definition: Accepting what happens without active response or resistance.
examples: Watching television is a fairly **passive** way to spend an evening.
He took a **passive** role and let others decide.

vocab.definition: Limiting people's freedom for their supposed own good, as a parent might.
examples: Some find the policy overly **paternalistic**.
A **paternalistic** government can stifle personal responsibility.

vocab.definition: A course of action or a route through life.
examples: Everyone has to find their own **path** in the end.
That decision set me on a completely different **path**.

vocab.definition: The capacity to accept delay or difficulty without frustration.
examples: Teaching children requires an enormous amount of **patience**.
My **patience** was wearing thin by the end of the queue.

vocab.definition: Able to accept delay or difficulty calmly.
examples: You have to be **patient** when learning a new skill.
She is remarkably **patient** with her students.

vocab.definition: Devotion to and support for one's country.
examples: Sporting events often stir a sense of **patriotism**.
Healthy **patriotism** should not slide into prejudice.

vocab.definition: Free from disturbance; calm and tranquil.
examples: The countryside is wonderfully **peaceful** at dawn.
I treasure a quiet, **peaceful** morning with a book.

vocab.definition: Human beings in general or considered collectively.
examples: What I love about the city is the sheer variety of **people**.
**People** tend to remember how you made them feel.

vocab.definition: Designed to be welcoming and easy for people to use or enjoy.
examples: The square was redesigned to be far more **people-friendly**.
A **people-friendly** city puts pedestrians before cars.

vocab.definition: Quick to notice or understand things.
examples: She made a very **perceptive** comment about my work.
Good writers are usually sharply **perceptive** observers.

vocab.definition: How well a person or thing does a task; a public presentation.
examples: Her **performance** in the interview was outstanding.
The orchestra gave a flawless **performance**.

vocab.definition: To spread through and be present in every part of something.
examples: A sense of optimism seemed to **permeate** the whole team.
Technology now **permeates** every aspect of daily life.

vocab.definition: To make something, especially something bad, continue indefinitely.
examples: Stereotypes in the media can **perpetuate** prejudice.
Such policies only **perpetuate** inequality.

vocab.definition: Persistence in doing something despite difficulty.
examples: It was sheer **perseverance** that got her through medical school.
Success in any field demands real **perseverance**.

vocab.definition: To continue in a course of action despite difficulty.
examples: You have to **persevere** even when progress feels slow.
They chose to **persevere** rather than give up.

vocab.definition: Continued despite difficulty or setbacks.
examples: She **persevered** through years of rejection before succeeding.
Against the odds, he **persevered** and finished the race.

vocab.definition: To continue firmly, or to go on existing.
examples: If the symptoms **persist**, you should see a doctor.
Old habits tend to **persist** long after we notice them.

vocab.definition: The quality of continuing steadily despite problems.
examples: Her quiet **persistence** eventually won everyone over.
Language learning rewards **persistence** above talent.

vocab.definition: Belonging to or affecting a particular person; private.
examples: That is a very **personal** decision only you can make.
I keep my **personal** life separate from work.

vocab.definition: Designed or adapted to suit a particular individual.
examples: Apps can now offer highly **personalised** recommendations.
A **personalised** study plan works far better for me.

vocab.definition: A particular way of viewing or thinking about something.
examples: Travel gives you a fresh **perspective** on your own life.
It helps to see the problem from another **perspective**.

vocab.definition: Spreading widely and present everywhere.
examples: Smartphones have a **pervasive** influence on young people.
There is a **pervasive** sense of anxiety about the future.

vocab.definition: Tending to expect the worst; lacking hope.
examples: I try not to be **pessimistic**, but the signs are worrying.
He has a rather **pessimistic** view of human nature.

vocab.definition: So frightened that one cannot move or think.
examples: I was **petrified** the first time I flew.
She stood **petrified** as the dog charged towards her.

vocab.definition: A distinct stage in a process of change or development.
examples: The early **phase** of any project is always the hardest.
It was just a **phase** I went through as a teenager.

vocab.definition: Visually charming or quaint, like a picture.
examples: We stayed in a **picturesque** village by the lake.
The old town is wonderfully **picturesque**.

vocab.definition: Of crucial importance in relation to how things develop.
examples: That internship was a **pivotal** moment in my career.
Teachers play a **pivotal** role in shaping young minds.

vocab.definition: The process of deciding in advance how to do something.
examples: Careful **planning** is what makes a trip run smoothly.
Poor **planning** was the real cause of the delay.

vocab.definition: Full of fun and good humour; light-hearted.
examples: He has a **playful** sense of humour that lifts the mood.
The design has a **playful**, colourful feel.

vocab.definition: Giving a sense of enjoyment or satisfaction; agreeable.
examples: We spent a **pleasant** afternoon by the river.
She has a warm and **pleasant** manner.

vocab.definition: A feeling of happy satisfaction and enjoyment.
examples: I take great **pleasure** in cooking for friends.
It was a real **pleasure** to meet you.

vocab.definition: Things that cause enjoyment or satisfaction.
examples: Simple **pleasures**, like a good coffee, matter most to me.
One of life's great **pleasures** is an unhurried morning.

vocab.definition: Stealing or taking goods by force, or exploiting resources greedily.
examples: Centuries of **plundering** stripped the region of its treasures.
We cannot keep **plundering** the planet's resources.

connectors.title: Adding information
connectors.note: Use these to pile on a further, supporting point.

items.use: Adds a stronger, separate point to what you have just said.
items.example: The plan is costly. **Furthermore**, it is unlikely to work.

items.use: Very similar to "furthermore"; adds an important extra point.
items.example: She is highly qualified; **moreover**, she has years of experience.

items.use: Neutral way to add a further point or item.
items.example: **In addition**, the service is available around the clock.

items.use: Adverb form; adds another fact or point.
Adds a point that strengthens the argument.
items.example: It is cheap, and **what is more**, it is reliable.

items.use: Adds a point, often a decisive extra reason.
items.example: I don't want to go; **besides**, it's too late.

items.use: Links two linked points, emphasising both.
items.example: It is **not only** efficient **but also** affordable.

items.use: Adds an item alongside another.
items.example: He teaches maths **as well as** physics.

items.use: Combines two factors into one effect.
items.example: Poor planning, **coupled with** bad weather, ruined the trip.

items.use: Informal way to add a further (often negative) point.
items.example: The flight was delayed, and **on top of that**, we lost a bag.

connectors.title: Contrast & opposition
connectors.note: Use these to signal a difference or an opposing idea.

items.use: The standard linker for a contrasting point.
items.example: The idea is bold. **However**, it carries real risks.

items.use: "In spite of that"; concedes a point then pushes on.
items.example: It was raining; **nevertheless**, the match went ahead.

items.use: Same meaning as "nevertheless"; slightly more formal.
items.example: The costs are high; **nonetheless**, the benefits justify them.

items.use: Introduces the opposite side of an argument.
items.example: Cars are convenient; **on the other hand**, they pollute.

items.use: Rejects a previous statement and asserts the opposite.
items.example: It was not dull; **on the contrary**, it was gripping.

items.use: Introduces an idea that is the reverse of the last one.
items.example: Cities offer jobs; **conversely**, they can feel isolating.

items.use: Highlights a clear difference between two things.
items.example: Sales rose in the city. **In contrast**, rural sales fell.

items.use: Directly compares two contrasting facts in one sentence.
items.example: He is cautious, **whereas** she takes risks.

items.use: Contrasts two clauses (also means "during").
items.example: **While** some enjoy routine, others crave change.

items.use: Signals a surprising contrast; "but".
"Despite that"; concedes then maintains a position.
items.example: The evidence is thin; **even so**, the idea is worth testing.

items.use: Followed by a noun or -ing; shows something happens anyway.
Very formal "despite".
Introduces a concession clause.
items.example: **Although** it was late, they carried on.

items.use: Signals a replacement or alternative choice.
items.example: Don't give up; **instead**, try a new approach.

connectors.title: Cause & reason
connectors.note: Use these to explain why something happens.

items.use: The everyday linker giving a direct reason.
items.example: We stayed in **because** it was pouring.

items.use: Gives a reason, usually one already known.
items.example: **Since** funds were limited, we cut the budget.

items.use: Gives a reason, slightly more formal than "because".
items.example: **As** the roads were closed, we turned back.

items.use: Followed by a noun; gives the cause of something.
items.example: The delay was **due to** heavy traffic.

items.use: Formal "because of"; followed by a noun.
items.example: **Owing to** the storm, flights were grounded.

items.use: Formal phrase introducing a cause.
items.example: The event was postponed **on account of** the weather.

items.use: "Considering the fact that"; sets up a reason.
items.example: **Given that** time is short, we must prioritise.

items.use: "Because of"; introduces a reason for a decision.
items.example: **In view of** the risks, the plan was dropped.

items.use: Gives an obvious reason; slightly informal.
items.example: **Seeing that** it's late, let's finish here.

connectors.title: Result & consequence
connectors.note: Use these to show the effect of something.

items.use: The standard linker introducing a logical result.
Formal "as a result"; often introduces a consequence.
items.example: The data was flawed; **thus**, the findings are unreliable.

items.use: Formal "for this reason"; introduces a result.
Introduces a direct consequence.
items.example: She missed the train; **consequently**, she was late.

items.use: Neutral way to show an outcome.
items.example: Costs fell, and **as a result**, profits grew.

items.use: Similar to "as a result"; slightly more formal.
items.example: The law changed; **as a consequence**, firms adapted.

items.use: "In a way that fits"; acts in response to a situation.
"For that reason"; links a status to its consequence.
items.example: He is a beginner and, **as such**, needs guidance.

items.use: Neutral, conversational way to give a reason-result link.
items.example: It rained all week; **that is why** the trip was cancelled.

connectors.title: Purpose
connectors.note: Use these to show the aim behind an action.

items.use: States the purpose of an action.
items.example: She studied hard **in order to** pass.

items.use: Formal way to express purpose.
items.example: He left early **so as to** avoid the rush.

items.use: Introduces a purpose clause with a verb.
items.example: Speak clearly **so that** everyone can follow.

items.use: Formal; followed by -ing, states an aim.
items.example: They met **with a view to** forming a partnership.

items.use: States a goal; followed by -ing.
items.example: The scheme was set up **with the aim of** cutting waste.

connectors.title: Sequence & order
connectors.note: Use these to order points or stages in time.

items.use: Orders a list of points in an argument.
items.example: **Firstly**, it is cheap; **secondly**, it is fast.

items.use: Introduces the first point or stage.
items.example: **To begin with**, we need a clear plan.

items.use: Formal "afterwards"; shows what came next.
items.example: He trained abroad and **subsequently** returned home.

items.use: "After that"; orders events in time.
items.example: We ate first and went out **afterwards**.

items.use: Formal way to introduce the next stage.
Shows something happening at the same time.
items.example: He cooked; **meanwhile**, I set the table.

items.use: Formal "before"; followed by a noun or -ing.
items.example: **Prior to** the meeting, we read the report.

items.use: "In the end, after some time."
Introduces the last point in a sequence.

connectors.title: Examples & illustration
connectors.note: Use these to introduce a supporting example.

items.use: The standard way to introduce an example.
items.example: Many cities, **for example** Tokyo, face overcrowding.

items.use: Introduces examples within a sentence.
Introduces a specific detail just mentioned.
Introduces an example to make a point clear.
items.example: **To illustrate**, consider the case of remote work.

items.use: Singles out one example for emphasis.
Emphasises one case above others.

connectors.title: Emphasis
connectors.note: Use these to stress or strengthen a point.

items.use: Confirms and strengthens a previous statement.
items.example: It was hard; **indeed**, it was the hardest year yet.

items.use: Adds a surprising or stronger truth.
items.example: It wasn't dull; **in fact**, it was fascinating.

items.use: Draws attention to a significant point.
items.example: Several countries, **notably** Japan, are ageing fast.

items.use: Marks the most important point.
States something as beyond doubt.
Flags a point as important or meaningful.
Formally flags a point the reader should register.
items.example: **It should be noted that** results may vary.

connectors.title: Comparison & similarity
connectors.note: Use these to show that two things are alike.

items.use: Shows a second case resembling the first.
items.example: Sales fell in the north; **similarly**, the south declined.

items.use: "In the same way"; links two similar ideas.
items.example: She works hard; **likewise**, her team does.

items.use: Draws a parallel between two situations.
items.example: **In the same way**, habits shape our days.

items.use: Signals two things are true to the same degree.
"For the same reason"; extends a line of thought.
items.example: He values trust; **by the same token**, he hates lies.

items.use: Sets two things side by side.
items.example: **Compared with** last year, costs are lower.

connectors.title: Condition
connectors.note: Use these to show something depends on a condition.

items.use: "Only if"; sets a firm condition.
items.example: You may go **provided that** you finish first.

items.use: States a condition that must hold.
items.example: It works **as long as** you follow the steps.

items.use: "If not"; states the exception.
items.example: We'll leave at six **unless** it rains.

items.use: Prepares for a possible situation.
items.example: Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.

items.use: Formal; states a strict requirement.
items.example: He agreed **on condition that** his name be kept private.

items.use: Shows something holds regardless of a condition.
items.example: I'll finish it **even if** it takes all night.

items.use: States what happens if a condition is not met.

connectors.title: Concession
connectors.note: Use these to admit a point before countering it.

items.use: Concedes a point before you argue against it.
items.example: **Admittedly**, the plan has flaws, but it is a start.

items.use: Accepts an opposing point briefly.
items.example: **Granted**, it is expensive, yet it lasts for years.

items.use: Concedes a fact before a "but".
items.example: **It is true that** risks exist, but they are manageable.

items.use: Formal concession followed by a clause.
items.example: **Despite the fact that** it rained, turnout was high.

items.use: Balances a concession against your own view.
items.example: **While it is true that** cars pollute, they aid mobility.

connectors.title: Clarification & restatement
connectors.note: Use these to restate an idea more clearly.

items.use: Restates an idea more simply.
items.example: It is non-refundable; **in other words**, you lose the money.

items.use: Introduces a clearer restatement.
items.example: He is frugal, **that is to say**, careful with money.

items.use: Rephrases a point from a new angle.
items.example: **To put it another way**, quality beats quantity.

items.use: Signals you are making a point clearer.
items.example: **To clarify**, the deadline is Friday, not Monday.

connectors.title: Generalisation
connectors.note: Use these to state what is usually or broadly true.

items.use: States what is true most of the time.
Gives an overall judgement.
items.example: **On the whole**, the response was positive.

items.use: Makes a general statement without exact detail.
items.example: **Broadly speaking**, the two plans are alike.

items.use: States a usual pattern.
items.example: **As a rule**, I avoid caffeine at night.

items.use: "Mostly"; gives a broad verdict.
"In most cases"; allows for exceptions.
items.example: **For the most part**, the service is reliable.

connectors.title: Conclusion & summary
connectors.note: Use these to close an argument or sum up.

items.use: Signals the final paragraph of an essay.
items.example: **In conclusion**, the benefits outweigh the costs.

items.use: Introduces a closing statement.
items.example: **To conclude**, change is both needed and overdue.

items.use: Introduces a brief recap.
items.example: **In summary**, three factors drive the trend.

items.use: Neutral way to summarise.
items.example: **To sum up**, planning saves both time and money.

items.use: Gives a final verdict after weighing both sides.
"Considering everything"; sums up overall.
items.example: **All in all**, it was a worthwhile experience.

items.use: Gives a judgement after weighing all factors.
items.example: **All things considered**, the plan is sound.

items.use: Points to the final, most important outcome.
